--- Page 1 ---
Asymptotic Optimality of 𝑐𝜇-Rule for LLM Inference Scheduling
under Memory Constraint
Zhenghao Li
HKUST
Shengbo Wang
University of Southern California
Nian Si
HKUST
Abstract
Large language model (LLM) inference, the process by which a pre-trained model receives an input
prompt and generates output tokens sequentially, has become increasingly important with the widespread
deployment of LLM-based applications. As inference workloads continue to scale, GPU memory has
emerged as a critical bottleneck: the long input prompts and generation sequences common in agentic and
reasoning workloads lead to substantial key–value (KV) cache usage. In this paper, we study the resulting
online scheduling problem from a queueing perspective. Requests arrive stochastically with heterogeneous
prompt and output lengths, undergo prefill and autoregressive decode, and compete for a finite KV-cache
capacity. Unlike classical queueing models, the duration of a processing step depends on both prefill
computation and KV-cache I/O, so service capacity is jointly determined by computation, memory access,
and memory occupancy. We develop a fluid model that reduces the system to a multiclass single-server
queue with effective service rates capturing computation, memory access, and memory capacity. This fluid
analysis yields a 𝑐𝜇priority rule, where the effective service rate 𝜇is jointly determined by computational
speed, memory bandwidth, and memory capacity. We prove that this rule minimizes cumulative holding
cost in the fluid model and, for a finite workload, also minimizes completion time and maximizes full-run
output-token throughput. We then construct a feasible scheduling policy for the original finite system and
prove that its scaled dynamics converge to the optimal fluid policy. Finally, experiments on a real LLM
serving engine using an NVIDIA H800 show that practical implementations of the proposed priority rule
substantially reduce average latency while maintaining high throughput relative to existing scheduling
policies.
1
Introduction
The public debut of ChatGPT in late 2022 marked a turning point in the swift adoption of generative artificial
intelligence, driven largely by advancements in large language models (LLMs) [7, 31, 34]. These systems have
rapidly integrated into routine workflows across research, education, industry, and entertainment [17, 21, 30],
facilitating billions of user interactions to date [16, 18]. However, alongside significant gains in human
productivity, this explosive growth has introduced critical bottlenecks in serving large-scale LLM inference
reliably and efficiently.
LLM inference refers to the process by which a pre-trained LLM receives an input prompt and generates
output tokens sequentially. Compared with traditional machine learning models, LLM inference is memory
and computation intensive, often involves long generation sequences, and can incur substantial latency
and resource costs. The importance of efficient inference is further amplified by the growing adoption of
reasoning models and test-time compute, which increase the amount of computation required for each request.
Deloitte1 estimates that inference will account for roughly two-thirds of total AI compute in 2026, up from
about one-third in 2023. Consequently, efficient LLM inference is not merely a problem of computational
1https://www.deloitte.com/us/en/insights/industry/technology/technology-media-and-telecom-predi
ctions/2026/compute-power-ai.html
1
arXiv:2611.04807v1  [math.OC]  3 Nov 2026


--- Page 2 ---
optimization, but a system-level challenge that requires carefully balancing responsiveness, throughput, and
resource costs.
Key-value (KV) caching [25, 32] has become a standard technique for accelerating LLM inference,
largely due to the extensive use of attention mechanisms [39]. Roughly speaking, the KV cache stores the
previously computed key and value representations of past tokens in GPU memory to avoid their repeated
computation when generating each new token. Thus, KV caching trades increased memory usage for reduced
computation and achieves substantially accelerated inference. However, this acceleration comes at the cost of
substantial GPU memory consumption and intensive memory access, making memory capacity and bandwidth
increasingly important. This becomes a severe issue for inference requests with long input contexts or long
generated sequences, which are increasingly common in agentic and reasoning workloads, making memory a
critical bottleneck in modern LLM inference [2].
In this paper, we study LLM inference with KV-cache memory constraints through an operations lens.
We abstract and model the inference scheduling task for LLMs as a multiclass queue. In this queueing system
model, inference requests arrive over time with heterogeneous workloads, characterized by their prompt and
output lengths, and a GPU server processes them according to prescribed dynamic scheduling decisions. The
workload each request brings to the system consists of two sequential phases that must be executed in order:
a prefill phase followed by an autoregressive decode phase. The scheduler dynamically determines which
requests are admitted and processed at each GPU time step. Our primary objective is to minimize the request
latency, or, equivalently, the cumulative number of unfinished requests in the system.
A crucial feature of LLM serving systems, and hence our queueing model, is the KV-cache constraint on
GPU memory capacity and bandwidth. As a request progresses through the prefill and decode stages, its KV
cache in GPU memory continues to grow until the request completes, while each processing step must also
access the KV states accumulated up to that point. These memory requirements can significantly affect the
number of requests that can be processed concurrently and the time required for each processing step. In
particular, GPU-step processing time depends on both the amount of prefill computation and the KV-cache
I/O volume, while the set of concurrently processed requests must satisfy a hard memory-capacity constraint.
To develop an efficient dynamic scheduling policy for this LLM inference queue, we consider a fluid
asymptotic regime in which the token processing rate and request arrival rate scale proportionally, while the
total memory capacity remains fixed. This choice of regime directly captures the key memory bottleneck in
LLM inference systems with KV caching, which shifts the primary computational burden toward memory
constraints and I/O costs.
The fluid approximation yields a tractable yet expressive limiting system with a familiar scheduling
structure. We show that, under the prescribed limiting regime, the memory-constrained LLM inference system
can be related to a classical multiclass queueing model with homogeneous servers. However, the effective
service rates in the fluid system must account for prefill computation, KV-cache I/O, and the effect of memory
capacity constraints on service availability. This motivates us to adapt the 𝑐𝜇priority rule [8, 28, 38], which
minimizes cumulative holding cost while maximizing full-run output-token throughput in the fluid model.
We establish that the 𝑐𝜇-rule remains optimal for this fluid system under the two-phase workload structure
and the memory constraint in the LLM serving system. Furthermore, to bridge the fluid control problem and
the prelimit LLM inference system, we construct a dynamic scheduling policy inspired by the 𝑐𝜇-rule. We
show that the proposed policy converges to the 𝑐𝜇-rule in the fluid limit and that the prelimit systems under
this policy converge to the proposed fluid system controlled by the 𝑐𝜇-rule.
Concretely, the paper makes the following main contributions.
• LLM system modeling. We develop a queueing model of LLM inference that explicitly accounts for
KV-cache memory capacity constraints and the associated memory I/O costs, with processing times
calibrated using real GPU measurements to capture their dependence on the composition of the scheduled
workload.
2


--- Page 3 ---
• Identifying the asymptotic regime. We identify a fluid regime in which processing and arrival rates
increase together while memory capacity remains fixed, preserving the system’s memory bottleneck. The
resulting model reveals a classical single-server scheduling structure with LLM-specific behaviors such as
two-phase workload and memory constraints.
• Asymptotic optimality of the 𝑐𝜇-rule. We prove that the 𝑐𝜇-rule minimizes cumulative holding cost and
maximizes full-run throughput for finite workloads in the fluid limit. To bridge the fluid and finite-system
models, we construct an implementable 𝑐𝜇-inspired policy and show that the resulting dynamics converge
to the optimal fluid limit.
• Numerical and real-system validation. We evaluate practical implementations of the proposed 𝑐𝜇-rule
using semi-synthetic workloads and real workload data on a real LLM serving engine. In both settings,
our policy demonstrates substantial reductions in average latency relative to the default scheduler while
maintaining high throughput.
Together, these results bridge classical queueing theory and priority-based scheduling policies with imple-
mentable, effective scheduling rules for modern LLM inference systems.
1.1
Related Work
Recent advances in LLM serving systems have enabled finer-grained control over batching and GPU memory
management. Yu et al. [47] developed iteration-level scheduling, allowing the batch to be reconstructed after
each model iteration. Kwon et al. [25] introduced PagedAttention, which stores KV caches in blocks to
reduce GPU memory waste and enable multiple requests to share cached data. Agrawal et al. [1] split long
prefill computations into smaller chunks and co-batched them with decode work. Together, these advances
provide the infrastructure for fine-grained control over batching and GPU memory management, serving as
both the foundation for our model and the practical testbed for our experiments.
To analyze LLM serving systems analytically, several pioneering studies have employed queueing models.
Dai et al. [11] characterize stable throughput under a per-batch token-budget constraint and establish the
throughput optimality of work-conserving policies, while Nie et al. [29] develop a fine-grained queueing
model that tracks KV-cache growth and establish stability and overload conditions for continuous batching
under the restrictive assumption of a constant batch processing time. Furthermore, Lin et al. [26] study
prefill–decode contention in multi-GPU settings and develop a scheduling policy that achieves asymptotically
optimal revenue as the number of GPUs grows, without explicitly modeling GPU memory-capacity constraints.
Recently, Yao et al. [46] study KV-cache reuse in multi-turn LLM conversations under a least-recently-used
(LRU) eviction policy and establish a mean-field limit for the cache hit ratio as the conversation arrival rate
and memory capacity scale proportionally.
The most relevant literature is Ao et al. [4] and Ao et al. [3]. For requests with known output lengths, Ao
et al. [4] propose WAIT to maximize throughput under a memory constraint. The policy waits for enough
requests of the same class to accumulate, then processes them together. However, setting these thresholds
requires arrival-rate information, and their extension to time-varying arrivals imposes additional load and
class-mix conditions. Moreover, obtaining valid parameters for WAIT requires certain load and memory
conditions to be satisfied, which may not hold in practical settings. We find that, although theoretically
optimal, WAIT’s performance can deteriorate in real-GPU implementations due to unnecessary idling. This
work models batch processing time only through KV-cache I/O, without considering the extra computation
time required to process tokens during the prefill phase. Ao et al. [3] further show that admitting requests
whenever memory is available can cause recurring evictions and throughput loss, and mitigate this via
rate-limited admission and request mixing, especially in multi-GPU deployments.
3


--- Page 4 ---
Besides queueing-based modeling, other studies approach this problem from an online linear programming
perspective: Jaillet et al. [23] develop a hindsight benchmark and the MC-SF algorithm, while Kong et al.
[24] propose the Smallest Volume First policy based on cumulative KV-cache usage. For offline scheduling,
prior work develops algorithms and evaluates their total completion time against a clairvoyant benchmark.
Specifically, Wang et al. [41] study the setting with known output lengths, Chen et al. [9] consider interval
predictions of output lengths, and Feng et al. [12, 13] develop algorithms that do not rely on output-length
predictions.
LLM inference under KV-cache memory constraints is closely related to stochastic bin packing, where
randomly arriving requests must be served subject to resource capacity constraints. Early studies establish
stability conditions for First-Fit and Best-Fit scheduling [10, 14]. In infinite-server models, greedy policies
with safety stocks [36], greedy randomized placement [37], and randomized Best-Fit [15] asymptotically
minimize the number of occupied servers. Stolyar [35] establishes asymptotic optimality of greedy allocation
for a convex approximation to the server-count objective. For a fixed number of servers, Maguluri et al.
[27] show that Best-Fit need not be throughput optimal and develop MaxWeight-based scheduling policies
with throughput guarantees. Gupta and Radovanovic [20] develop Lagrangian-based packing algorithms for
permanent and departing requests, including a model with configuration-dependent service slowdowns.
Despite similar constraints and objectives, LLM inference scheduling differs from classical stochastic
bin-packing problems in several ways. First, while stochastic bin-packing models assume that each request
has a fixed size upon arrival, the KV-cache usage of an LLM request grows as generation progresses. Second,
LLM inference involves two distinct phases, prefill and decode, with different memory dynamics. Third,
whereas service times in classical stochastic bin-packing models are typically independent of current memory
occupancy, processing times in LLM inference depend on memory usage due to KV-cache I/O costs.
The objective of minimizing cumulative holding cost connects our problem to the literature on 𝑐𝜇priority
scheduling. Buyukkoc et al. [8] establish the optimality of the 𝑐𝜇rule for a preemptive single-server queue
with linear holding costs, geometric service times, and a general arrival process. Van Mieghem [38] extends
this framework to convex delay costs and establishes the asymptotic optimality of a generalized 𝑐𝜇rule in
heavy traffic. Mandelbaum and Stolyar [28] further extend the analysis to heterogeneous servers and prove
heavy-traffic asymptotic optimality under complete resource pooling. Zychlinski et al. [48] study queues
in which jobs may require multiple servers simultaneously and establish the asymptotic optimality of an
idle-avoid 𝑐𝜇/𝑚policy in a many-server regime. Their model is related to ours through resource constraints,
but differs in three key aspects: in LLM inference, a job’s resource usage (KV cache) grows during service,
service rates depend on the types and numbers of jobs processed together, and memory capacity remains
𝑀= 𝑂(1), so each job’s resource requirement is non-negligible relative to total capacity.
The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we present our queueing model for
LLM inference. In Section 4, we establish the optimality of the 𝑐𝜇rule for the fluid model. In Section 5, we
construct a feasible policy for the discrete system and prove that its scaled dynamics converge to those under
the optimal fluid policy. Section 6 presents real GPU experiments that validate our theoretical results. Finally,
we conclude the paper and discuss limitations and directions for future work in Section 7.
2
LLM Inference Systems
We consider an online LLM inference system in which user requests arrive stochastically over time and wait
in a queue for service on a single GPU. Each arriving request contains an input prompt and asks the model to
generate an output sequence. A scheduler determines which requests are processed by the GPU over time.
The processing of each request consists of a prefill phase followed by an autoregressive decode phase.
During the prefill phase, the model processes the prompt tokens and constructs their attention key–value
(KV) states. With chunked prefill, the input prompt is divided into several smaller chunks that are processed
4


--- Page 5 ---
sequentially and the first output token is generated when the final chunk is processed. During the decode
phase, the model generates the remaining output tokens one at a time. Each decode step takes the latest output
token as input, appends its KV state, and generates the next output token. The request’s KV cache occupies
GPU memory throughout execution and is released upon completion. Figure 1 summarizes this lifecycle.

Figure 1: Lifecycle of a request with prompt length 𝑠𝑗= 4, output length 𝑜𝑗= 3, and two-token prefill chunks. The
first prefill step processes 𝑃1, 𝑃2 and writes their keys and values to the KV cache without emitting an output token.
The final prefill step processes 𝑃3, 𝑃4, writes their keys and values to the cache, and emits 𝑂1. Each decode step takes
the latest output token as input, appends its keys and values to the cache, and emits the next token. After the request
completes, its KV cache is released.
Modern inference engines use a GPU step as the smallest unit of scheduling. At each GPU step, a batch is
formed from requests that may be at different stages of execution. After the step completes, the scheduler
updates request states and may re-form the next batch from eligible waiting and running requests; requests
may therefore enter or leave the scheduled batch between GPU steps. This mechanism is commonly called
continuous batching [47]. Modern engines may also use mixed prefill–decode batching, in which a GPU step
processes prefill work from some requests and decode work from others [1].
Every processed token contributes KV states, so a request’s KV-cache occupancy grows during prefill and
then by one token at each decode step. The running requests share a finite GPU KV-cache capacity, which we
measure in tokens. Figure 2 illustrates how the scheduled batch changes at GPU-step boundaries.
Our queueing model represents request progress through its prefill and decode stages. Requests are
partitioned into 𝐽classes. A class-𝑗request has known prompt length 𝑠𝑗and output length 𝑜𝑗. The GPU
has KV-cache capacity 𝑀tokens. Each prompt is partitioned into chunks of size 𝑐chunk. Accordingly, we
define the number of prefill chunks of a class-𝑗request by 𝐿𝑗=
l

first output token. If 𝑜𝑗= 1, the request leaves the system immediately after its final prefill stage.
Let 𝑚(𝑡) denote the maximum KV-cache usage during step 𝑡. It consists of the KV states already
occupying GPU memory and those newly written during the step. The memory constraint is

this volume counts the existing KV states accessed by the batch and the new KV states written during the step.
By empirically testing different mixed batches on an NVIDIA H800, we observe that the step time (batch
processing time) varies approximately linearly with both KV-cache I/O volume and the number of prompt
tokens processed. Figure 3 shows these linear relationships.

3
System Modeling and Fluid Regime
In this section, we formulate a sequence of prelimit queueing models for the LLM inference system and
derive the corresponding fluid control problem. We first specify the system state, queueing dynamics, control
decisions, and memory constraints. We then apply fluid scaling and formulate the corresponding fluid control
problem. Finally, we show that the fluid control problem also exhibits a state-space collapse phenomenon
commonly observed in the queueing literature [6, 44].

3.1

caching techniques that trade memory capacity and I/O cost for computation speed in modern LLM inference
systems. Concretely, for the step-time model in (1), we assume that the positive coefficients of the 𝑟th system

The arrival processes are modeled as nonhomogeneous Poisson processes, with arrival rates scaled by a
factor of 𝑟to match the processing-time scaling. Specifically, let 𝜆𝑟

3.2
Fluid Scaling
Within an 𝑂(1) unit of clock time in the 𝑟th system, since the arrival rates scale as 𝑂(𝑟) and each GPU
step takes 𝑂(1/𝑟) units of clock time, cumulative arrivals, cumulative stage completions, and waiting-queue
lengths can all be of order 𝑂(𝑟). This suggests the following scaling, which we use to restore stability and
obtain a sensible limiting system. For 𝜉∈R+, define

Here 𝜉= 𝑡/𝑟is fluid-scaled step time. When limits of these scaled processes exist, we omit the bars and the
index 𝑟and write the limiting processes as 𝑝, 𝑑, U, V, and 𝑓. The formal convergence from the prelimit
system to the fluid limit is established in Section 5.
A crucial phenomenon as a consequence of of this fluid regime and the memory constraint stems from
the following observation. For 𝑘= 1, . . . , 𝐿𝑗−1, each request counted by 𝑝𝑟
𝑗,𝑘occupies 𝑐chunk(𝐿𝑗−𝑘)
KV-cache slots. Likewise, for 𝑘= 1, . . . , 𝑜𝑗−1, each request counted by 𝑑𝑟
𝑗,𝑘occupies 𝑠𝑗+ 𝑜𝑗−𝑘−1
KV-cache slots. Since the total capacity 𝑀is fixed independently of 𝑟, the memory constraint bounds each of
these unscaled states by a constant independent of 𝑟. Therefore,
¯𝑝𝑟
𝑗,𝑘(𝜉) ≤
𝑀
𝑟𝑐chunk(𝐿𝑗−𝑘) →0
and
¯𝑑𝑟
𝑗,𝑘(𝜉) ≤
𝑀
𝑟(𝑠𝑗+ 𝑜𝑗−𝑘−1) →0.
(8)
Thus, every fluid-scaled intermediate-stage state vanishes as 𝑟→∞. The fluid-scaled waiting-queue length
¯𝑝𝑟
𝑗,𝐿𝑗need not vanish because waiting requests do not occupy GPU memory. This observation naturally leads
to the phenomenon of stage-level state-space collapse, yielding a more tractable limiting system for which we
can characterize an optimal policy. We provide a detailed characterization of this phenomenon in Section 3.4.
As a result, on every bounded horizon, the normalized holding-cost contribution of requests in intermediate
stages vanishes. Thus, although J 𝑟counts all requests in the system, its fluid counterpart contains only the
waiting-queue lengths 𝑝𝑗,𝐿𝑗.
The cumulative stage completions need not vanish with these states. A fixed fluid-time interval [𝜉1, 𝜉2]
contains 𝑂(𝑟) GPU steps. Since each step can complete 𝑂(1) requests at a given stage, the cumulative
number of stage completions over the interval can be 𝑂(𝑟). After division by 𝑟, the corresponding cumulative
flow can therefore remain 𝑂(1).
3.3
Fluid Control Problem
We now formulate the limiting fluid control problem driven by the arrival rates 𝜆𝑗. Fluid evolution is indexed
by step time 𝜉∈R+, the continuous analogue of the discrete GPU-step index, whereas 𝜏∈R+ still represents
clock time. Under a policy 𝜋, the real-time clock 𝑓𝜋maps step time 𝜉to clock time 𝜏= 𝑓𝜋(𝜉).
At step time 𝜉, 𝑝𝑗,𝑘(𝜉) ∈R+ is the fluid-scaled number of class-𝑗requests with 𝑘prefill chunks remaining,
and 𝑑𝑗,𝑘(𝜉) ∈R+ is the fluid-scaled number of class-𝑗requests with 𝑘decode tokens remaining. The system
state is,

Definition 2 impose three sets of constraints that reflect the requirements for prelimit policies in Definition
1. First, the (deterministic) fluid cumulative control processes U and V must start from zero and be
nondecreasing. Second, the per-step memory constraint 𝑚𝑟(𝑡) ≤𝑀in the prelimit model translates into the
Lipschitz constraint (10) in the fluid model. The left-hand side measures the cumulative KV-cache usage
associated with work completed during (𝜉2, 𝜉1], which cannot exceed 𝑀(𝜉1 −𝜉2), the memory capacity
integrated over the interval. Third, the nonnegativity of the prelimit queues is preserved in the fluid limit,
while the convergence in (8) implies that all intermediate-stage fluid states must vanish.

Remark 1. Since 𝑏> 0 and the cumulative controls of an admissible policy are continuous and nondecreasing,

measure 𝑑𝑓𝜋. All integrals with respect to 𝑑𝑓𝜋below are understood in this sense.
Since admissibility implies that all intermediate-stage states are zero, the fluid control problem considers
the analogue of the prelimit objective (7), seeking an admissible policy 𝜋that minimizes

4
Optimal Control of the Fluid Model
In this section, we study the 𝑐𝜇priority policy for the fluid model. We first introduce the basic idea of the
𝑐𝜇rule and define the effective service rate 𝜇𝑗. We then describe the fluid 𝑐𝜇policy and establish that it
minimizes the cumulative holding cost. Finally, we show that the policy also minimizes the completion time
and, consequently, maximizes the full-run output-token throughput.
4.1
Effective Service Rates and the 𝑐𝜇Rule
The fluid control objective (12) can be viewed as a linear holding cost on the queue lengths of waiting requests.
Each unit of waiting class-𝑗requests incurs a holding cost at rate 𝑐𝑗. Serving class-𝑗requests at rate 𝜇𝑗
therefore reduces the holding-cost rate by 𝑐𝑗𝜇𝑗per unit of time. This motivates the classical 𝑐𝜇rule, which
prioritizes classes in decreasing order of 𝑐𝑗𝜇𝑗. To apply this rule to our fluid model and establish its optimality,
we first identify the effective service rates determined by the memory constraint and the step-time model.
Consider an interval during which only class 𝑗is served. The memory constraint in (17) gives, in
differential form, that ˜𝑚𝑗𝑑X 𝜋
𝑗(𝜉) ≤𝑀𝑑𝜉. Hence the class-𝑗service rate in step time is at most 𝑀/ ˜𝑚𝑗, with
equality when the KV capacity is saturated. At this saturated service rate, the amount of class-𝑗service
completed per unit of step time is 𝑀/ ˜𝑚𝑗, while the corresponding elapsed clock time is
␀𝑎pf𝑠𝑗+ 𝑎kv ˜𝑚𝑗

We apply the 𝑐𝜇rule using these effective service rates and index the classes so that
𝑐1𝜇1 ≥𝑐2𝜇2 ≥· · · ≥𝑐𝐽𝜇𝐽.
The policy allocates service in this priority order, serving each class at the maximum rate permitted by
its waiting requests, new arrivals, and the memory constraint (17), and passing any remaining capacity to
lower-priority classes. For a more detailed characterization of the 𝑐𝜇rule and its generalizations, see for
example Buyukkoc et al. [8].
4.2
Holding-Cost Optimality
We measure the GPU’s service budget in units of clock time: an interval of length Δ𝜏provides Δ𝜏units of
budget. Since 𝜇𝑗is the effective service rate of class 𝑗, processing 𝑥class-𝑗requests requires 𝑥/𝜇𝑗units of
effective work. At each time, the fluid 𝑐𝜇policy considers classes in decreasing order of 𝑐𝑗𝜇𝑗. For each class,
it uses the available budget to serve waiting requests and new arrivals, then passes any remaining budget to the
next class. To establish the holding-cost optimality of the 𝑐𝜇rule, we use cumulative completion processes to
represent the policy and construct these processes recursively in priority order.
For this recursive construction, let 𝐴𝑗(𝜏) denote the cumulative class-𝑗arrivals by clock time 𝜏:

5
Fluid-Limit Convergence
In this section, we demonstrate that the optimal fluid 𝑐𝜇policy provides operational guidance for the prelimit
𝑟th system. We construct a smoothed 𝑐𝜇-inspired dynamic policy that is admissible at every finite scale 𝑟. At
a high level, it follows the 𝑐𝜇priority order when forming admission plans and spreads each plan over a short
window to satisfy the KV-cache capacity constraint. In particular, this policy does not require knowledge of
the arrival rates 𝜆𝑗(·). Then, we show that under this policy and fluid scaling, the prelimit system and control
converge to the fluid system and control under the optimal 𝑐𝜇policy.
To track the memory used by a request that runs continuously after admission, define the reserved
KV-cache usage of a class-𝑗request at the start of the GPU step occurring ℎsteps after admission by

0, otherwise.

Remark 3. The choice 𝑤𝑟= max{𝐻kv + 1, ⌈√𝑟⌉} satisfies the required conditions. The condition 𝑤𝑟→∞
smooths the step-level admission plans, whereas 𝑤𝑟/𝑟→0 ensures that the smoothing window vanishes in
fluid time. At step 𝑡, 𝑦𝑟
𝑗(𝑡) specifies how many class-𝑗requests are assigned an admission plan. Equation (34)
schedules 𝑦𝑟

out over a 𝑤𝑟-step window. Once admitted, each request runs continuously until completion; its subsequent

written using the waiting-queue length as

plans are not included when a new plan is formed.
The following proposition establishes the admissibility of the policy in the prelimit queueing model.
Proposition 1 (Admissibility). Suppose that, initially, some requests may be waiting, but no requests are
being processed on the GPU. Then, the policy in Definition 5 is admissible for the prelimit queueing model.
Proposition 1 establishes policy admissibility at every finite scale. Its proof is deferred to Appendix F.
We next show that the smoothed 𝑐𝜇-inspired policy converges under fluid scaling to the fluid 𝑐𝜇policy.
Theorem 3 (Fluid-limit convergence). Suppose initially no requests are being processed on the GPU, and the
initial waiting queue lengths satisfy

It is holding-cost optimal by Theorem 1 and completion-time and throughput optimal by Theorem 2. Thus,
the smoothing used at finite scale disappears under fluid scaling, and the real-time clock, system states, and
the fluid-scaled cumulative stage-completion processes converge uniformly on compacts in probability to the
optimal fluid trajectory.
6
Numerical Experiments
In this section, we evaluate two practical implementations of the 𝑐𝜇ordering on a real LLM serving engine.
We conduct semi-synthetic experiments using prompt lengths, decode lengths, and arrival rates derived from
a real-world dataset [40].
18


--- Page 19 ---
6.1
Experimental Setup
We run Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct [19] using vLLM [25], with each run using a single NVIDIA H800 GPU.
Within each experimental group, all policies are run sequentially on the same GPU. We calibrate the
step-time model separately for each GPU to estimate 𝑎pf, 𝑎kv, and 𝑏. Substituting these estimates and request
𝑖’s prompt and output lengths into the effective-service-rate formula (18) gives its estimated service rate b𝜇𝑖
for the 𝑐𝜇ordering.
We use the To-B, To-C, Thinking, and Coder traces from the Qwen-Bailian Anonymous Dataset [40].
To-B covers business-facing API calls and task automation, while To-C covers consumer-facing interactive
chat. Thinking focuses on reasoning-intensive chat, and Coder covers code generation and interactive
programming. These anonymized production traces each cover a two-hour period. Each record provides a
relative arrival time and prompt and output lengths. We retain only requests whose combined prompt and
output lengths do not exceed the 8K-token context window of Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct. We adjust the
arrival rates to achieve a traffic intensity of approximately 0.95. For replay, we configure the LLM engine to
generate exactly the specified number of output tokens for each request. Table 2 summarizes their lengths and
eligible request counts.
Table 2: Eligible requests in the four production traces. Prompt and output lengths are measured in tokens.

Figure 5 compares the joint prompt–output length distributions. On average, To-B has the shortest
prompts and outputs, followed by To-C. Thinking and Coder have similarly long prompts, but Thinking has
substantially longer outputs, consistent with its focus on long-form reasoning. We use To-B to construct the
semi-synthetic workloads in Section 6.3, and replay all four traces after time compression in Section 6.4.
6.2
Policies and Performance Measures
Based on the 𝑐𝜇priority rule, we implement two practical scheduling policies: 𝑐𝜇and 𝑐𝜇-backfill. We
compare them with the default vLLM scheduler, MC-SF [23], SVF [24], and WAIT-frac, a fractional
implementation of WAIT [4]. The 𝑐𝜇, 𝑐𝜇-backfill, MC-SF, and SVF policies order waiting requests by
priority. All policies except the default vLLM scheduler use nonpreemptive implementations and assume that
each request’s output length is known.
These nonpreemptive policies check future KV-cache usage before admission, accounting for cache
growth and memory released upon completion. A request is admitted only if the total KV-cache usage will
remain within 𝑀at every future GPU step.
Using the future KV-cache feasibility check, the 𝑐𝜇policy scans waiting requests in decreasing 𝑐𝑖b𝜇𝑖order
and stops at the first infeasible request. The 𝑐𝜇-backfill policy uses the same ordering and feasibility check.
When a request cannot be admitted immediately, the policy uses the future KV-cache feasibility check to find
its earliest feasible future admission step and assumes that the request is admitted at that step in subsequent
checks. It then continues scanning lower-priority requests, admitting a request immediately if the feasibility
check is satisfied with all these planned admissions included. Figure 6 illustrates this procedure. Both policies
are nonpreemptive and continuously serve admitted requests until completion.

Figure 6: Illustrative KV-cache profiles for reservations and backfilling. The blue area shows 10 resident or already
selected requests. The orange, purple, and red areas add three reserved requests, each with 512 output tokens, starting at
𝑡+ 200, 𝑡+ 360, and 𝑡+ 560, respectively. The green area adds a smaller backfill request with 400 output tokens at
𝑡. KV-cache usage grows as tokens are generated and drops at completion. The combined usage remains below 𝑀,
preserving all three reserved starts.
MC-SF orders waiting requests by increasing output length 𝑜𝑖, while SVF orders them by increasing
cumulative KV-cache volume 𝑠𝑖𝑜𝑖+ 𝑜𝑖(𝑜𝑖+ 1)/2. Both use nonpreemptive implementations with the same
future KV-cache feasibility check. When 𝑐𝑖= 1, 𝑎pf = 0, and prefill is not chunked, the 𝑐𝜇rule reduces to a
volume-based priority rule, as in SVF.
The vanilla version of WAIT described in [4] uses positive integer service quotas for each class and stage,
so the smallest positive quota is one request per GPU step. When the quota is one, a single waiting request
is sufficient to make its class eligible for service in the next GPU step, eliminating the intended waiting
mechanism for request accumulation. In our experiments, however, matching class-wise arrival rates may
require service quotas below one request per GPU step. We therefore introduce WAIT-frac, which maintains
fractional credits separately for each class and stage. Serving one request at a stage consumes one unit of
credit; fractional remainders carry over to subsequent steps, subject to an expiry rule. Runtime KV-cache
checks enforce memory feasibility.
In WAIT-frac, the reference step time 𝑇WAIT converts class-wise arrival rates into the credit increments for
each GPU step. Under our GPU configuration, the original parameter formula for WAIT does not yield a
positive value of 𝑇WAIT, because Ao et al. [4] assumes a different batch service-time model. We therefore set
𝑇WAIT = 120 ms, chosen to be comparable to the GPU-step time at peak load.

6.3
Semi-Synthetic Workloads
We estimate a Gaussian mixture model to cluster eligible To-B requests into 16 classes. For each class, we
generate Poisson arrivals with time-varying rates based on the source trace and rescale the arrival times to
attain a traffic intensity of 0.95. We then assume that all requests within each class have identical prompt and
decode lengths, given by their respective cluster centers. We repeat the experiment eight times, replaying the
same generated trace for every policy within each repetition.
Table 3 summarizes all eight repetitions. The 𝑐𝜇-backfill policy has the lowest mean latency, mean TTFT,
and mean clearance time, and the highest mean output-token throughput. The 𝑐𝜇policy also achieves low
mean latency, only slightly above 𝑐𝜇-backfill and below all other baselines. WAIT-frac has the lowest mean
P99 latency, showing that the ranking can differ between average and tail latency.
Table 3: Results on eight semi-synthetic traces. Average latency and clearance are mean ± sample standard deviation;

Bold values are best among the reported policies.

6.4
Real Production Traces
We next evaluate the policies on To-B, To-C, Thinking, and Coder while retaining their original request
sequences. For each eligible source trace, we multiply all relative arrival times by a common factor to attain a
traffic intensity of 0.95. This changes the arrival rate while preserving the request order, relative interarrival
gaps, and each prompt–output length pair. The length distributions are therefore those shown in Figure 5;
Figure 7 shows the time-varying arrival rate of To-B after compression. We report one run per policy for each
source trace, with all policies replaying the same compressed trace.
Table 4 summarizes the results on the four compressed traces. On To-B, both 𝑐𝜇policies achieve lower
average latency and mean TTFT than the baselines, with 𝑐𝜇-backfill performing best. On To-C and Coder,
𝑐𝜇-backfill, 𝑐𝜇, and SVF have similar average latency and mean TTFT. On Thinking, 𝑐𝜇achieves the lowest
average latency and mean TTFT.

7
Conclusion and Future Work
In this paper, we propose a simple modification of the 𝑐𝜇rule and establish its asymptotic optimality for LLM
inference scheduling under memory constraints. Interesting directions for future research include extending
the queueing model to multi-GPU settings and agentic workloads, as well as investigating the impact of
output-length prediction errors on scheduling performance.

Non-Anticipativity of Prelimit Policies
Fix 𝑟≥1 and an initial state 𝑧𝑟

with the usual augmentation. A prelimit policy is non-anticipative if, at every GPU step 𝑡, all control
increments ΔU𝑟
𝑗,𝑘(𝑡) and ΔV𝑟
𝑗,𝑘(𝑡) are measurable with respect to G𝑟
𝑡:= F 𝑟
𝑓𝑟(𝑡).
We show by induction that 𝑓𝑟(𝑡) is a stopping time with respect to {F 𝑟
𝜏: 𝜏≥0} for every 𝑡∈Z+. First,
𝑓𝑟(0) = 0 is a stopping time.
Suppose that 𝑓𝑟(𝑛) is a stopping time for every 𝑛= 0, . . . , 𝑡. By the non-anticipativity condition, the
control increments ΔU𝑟
𝑗,𝑘(𝑡) and ΔV𝑟
𝑗,𝑘(𝑡), over their respective prefill and decode stages, are G𝑟
𝑡-measurable.
The step duration Δ𝑟(𝑡) is a function of these increments, so 𝑓𝑟(𝑡+ 1) = 𝑓𝑟(𝑡) + Δ𝑟(𝑡) is also G𝑟
𝑡-measurable.
For every 𝜏≥0, the event {Δ𝑟(𝑡) ≤𝜏−𝑓𝑟(𝑡)} belongs to G𝑟
𝑡= F 𝑟
𝑓𝑟(𝑡). By the definition of F 𝑟
𝑓𝑟(𝑡),
intersecting this event with { 𝑓𝑟(𝑡) ≤𝜏} gives an event in F 𝑟
𝜏. Since Δ𝑟(𝑡) ≥0, we obtain
{ 𝑓𝑟(𝑡+ 1) ≤𝜏} = { 𝑓𝑟(𝑡) ≤𝜏, Δ𝑟(𝑡) ≤𝜏−𝑓𝑟(𝑡)} ∈F 𝑟
𝜏.
Thus, 𝑓𝑟(𝑡+ 1) is a stopping time, completing the induction. Consequently, G𝑟
𝑡= F 𝑟
𝑓𝑟(𝑡) is well-defined for
every 𝑡.
B
Illustration of the Fluid 𝑐𝜇Policy under General Arrivals
Figure 8 illustrates the policy for three classes with 𝑐1𝜇1 > 𝑐2𝜇2 > 𝑐3𝜇3. Here, X∗
𝑗,rt(𝜏) denotes the
cumulative number of class-𝑗completions by clock time 𝜏. During [0, 2], the class-1 backlog receives all
available service, while lower-priority classes wait. During [6, 9], class-1 requests are served as they arrive,
using only part of the service budget; the remainder is used to serve the class-2 backlog. During [9, 11], the
policy keeps up with arrivals to both classes 1 and 2 and allocates the remaining budget to class 3.

Remark 5 (Workload interpretation). The queue length 𝑝𝜋
𝑗,𝐿𝑗records the number of waiting class-𝑗requests.
We use the effective service rate 𝜇𝑗to convert this quantity into real-time units, so 𝑊𝜋
ℓmeasures the total
effective workload of waiting requests in the first ℓclasses. Applying the same conversion to cumulative
arrivals, 𝑔ℓdescribes the net workload input to these classes. Since unused service capacity cannot be saved
for future arrivals, the Skorokhod reflection 𝜑ℓgives the remaining workload when the full service capacity
is devoted to these classes whenever they have work waiting. This yields the smallest remaining workload
permitted by the available capacity, and hence a lower bound on 𝑊𝜋
ℓat the corresponding clock time.

G
Proof of Theorem 3
We first show that the moving average and the fixed stage delays produce vanishing errors under fluid scaling,
so it suffices to analyze the cumulative planned-admission processes and the clock approximation constructed
from them (Lemma 3). We then establish joint 𝐶-tightness and show that every subsequential limit satisfies
the fluid model’s queue nonnegativity constraints, memory constraint, and clock equation (Lemma 4). The
key step is to recover the priority rule in the limit: on any interval where a class’s waiting-queue length
is positive, its priority prefix uses the full capacity and the corresponding residual service budget remains
constant. This yields the reflection representation that identifies every subsequential limit with the fluid 𝑐𝜇
policy (Lemma 5).
We begin by defining the auxiliary processes used throughout the proof.

Remark 6 (Interpretation of the prelimit estimates).
(i) Equations (61) and (62) give memory-based upper bounds on both the class-𝑗planned-admission
amount 𝑦𝑟
𝑗(𝑡) and the admission increment ΔU𝑟
𝑗,𝐿𝑗(𝑡) at each step 𝑡. Equation (63) states that the plans
for all classes share one memory-based planning budget.
(ii) Equation (64) shows that the difference between the fluid-scaled cumulative planned admissions ¯𝑃𝑟
𝑗(𝜉)
and the fluid-scaled cumulative admissions U𝑟
𝑗,𝐿𝑗(⌊𝑟𝜉⌋)/𝑟vanishes uniformly on compact step-time
intervals. Thus, spreading each plan over 𝑤𝑟steps has a negligible effect on cumulative admissions at
the fluid scale.
(iii) The prefill-stage delay bound (65) and the decode-stage delay bound (66) show that the fixed delays
between admission and later stages disappear under fluid scaling. The fluid-scaled cumulative stage-
completion processes U𝑟
𝑗,𝑘(⌊𝑟𝜉⌋)/𝑟and V𝑟
𝑗,𝑘(⌊𝑟𝜉⌋)/𝑟are therefore asymptotically equivalent to the
fluid-scaled cumulative admission process U𝑟
𝑗,𝐿𝑗(⌊𝑟𝜉⌋)/𝑟.
(iv) The clock approximation in (67) uses the fluid-scaled cumulative planned admissions ¯𝑃𝑟
𝑗(𝜉) to
approximate the real-time clock ¯𝑓𝑟(𝜉).
